summary.text:
Avon Fire Authority's Treasury Management Strategy review for the year ending March 2026 is a nine-page annual outturn to the Fire Authority on 1 July 2026, with a two-page Prudential Indicators appendix (5623) held separately. The book is small and stationary: £7.00m of PWLB at 3.16% across two fixed-rate maturity loans, unchanged all year — no draws, no maturities, no rescheduling. Our file ties to the basis point: PW503793 £3.5m at 2.99% maturing March 2030 and PW503794 £3.5m at 3.33% maturing March 2040, weighted mean 3.16% deriving cleanly from those two rates.

The interesting numbers sit forward, not backward. Appendix 1 contains a Liability Benchmark chart 2023/24–2028/29 not narrated in the main paper's prose: Loans CFR rises from around £10m today to roughly £40m by 2028/29, a fourfold increase over three years, implying roughly £30m of new borrowing on top of the current £7m book. £11.8m of that has already been deferred once — Appendix 1 shows approved 2025/26 borrowing of £18,800k against actual £7,000k, the whole £11.8m variance driven by £10.75m of capex slippage (approved £14,655k vs actual £3,902k, most of it Bath Station rebuild delays). Set against the paper's own 2025/26 PWLB range (5-year averaged 4.82%, 25-year 6.06%) versus the existing 3.16% weighted book, the blended cost of debt is heading materially higher.

Balance-sheet identity ties in three independent presentations: CFR £10.05m − PWLB £7.00m − OLTL £0.93m = £2.12m internal borrowing, matching the main paper's under-borrowing figure of (£2.13m) and Appendix 1's deferred borrowing line of £2,124k, all to £0.01m of rounding. Investment side is fully outsourced to Bristol City Council on a SONIA-less-0.25% basis (no direct counterparties); the £365k of income beat the £250k budget by £115k, attributed to capex slippage keeping cash balances higher for longer.

Contact block (§10, p9) prints only 'Verity Truscott, Statutory Finance Officer' with no email address. Draft written and machine-checked — the recipient line is the only outstanding gap. Meeting on 1 July has passed; next expected treasury paper is the November 2026 mid-year review.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every authority's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every authority in the country, so we can see how a set of figures compares with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your Treasury Management Strategy review presented to the Fire Authority on 1 July, ahead of the next treasury paper. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper is clean, internally consistent, and the Appendix 1 indicators sheet spells the CFR path out properly; this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The quickest check first. Paragraph 4.3 prints your PWLB book at £7.00m weighted 3.16%. Our file gives £7,000,000 at 3.16% across two maturity loans, and the individual maturities land in the same two buckets you print at paragraph 4.4 — one £3.5m in the 2-5 year band (maturing 5 March 2030 at 2.99%) and one £3.5m over ten years (maturing 5 March 2040 at 3.33%). Weighted mean 3.16% derives cleanly from those two rates and settles the question of whether we're looking at the same book.

Two things follow. Both loans are legacy — 2.99% and 3.33% both sit well below the 2025/26 PWLB range you print at §5.5, where five-year averaged 4.82%, ten-year 5.38% and twenty-five year 6.06%. On the DMO's premature repayment curve as at 14 August, both loans sit at a discount, with an indicative settlement of £6.23m against £7.0m principal — around £773k, or roughly 11% of principal. That is indicative only. Only the DMO can quote a binding figure, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and whether anything is worth doing turns on replacement borrowing cost. It's the position priced daily, not advice. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The more consequential number in the pack sits in Appendix 1's Liability Benchmark chart, and it's the one your main paper's prose doesn't narrate. The existing book runs off no maturities before 2030, but Loans CFR rises steeply from around £10m today to roughly £40m by 2028/29 — a fourfold increase over three years, with roughly £30m of new borrowing implied on top of the current £7m book. £11.8m of that was in the 2025/26 approved column and has already been deferred once (Appendix 1 shows Borrowing approved 18,800 against actual 7,000, driven by £10.75m of capex slippage). Set against the 2025/26 PWLB range averaging 4.82% to 6.06% across the medium-to-long end versus the existing 3.16% weighted book, that forward path is a materially higher blended cost of debt than the current position.

Which is where two of our pages become useful. Loan-analysis prices the two current loans against the DMO curve every day. pwlb-activity carries what the rest of the sector is drawing month by month, so you can see whether the borrowing windows are opening or thinning as the deferred requirement lands — worth watching once the mid-year review starts to firm up the 2026/27 plan.

None of it needs a subscription, and the daily rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check. On training, three fit Avon Fire particularly well: our liability benchmark pathway — interactive, built on live data, plots your CFR against forecast investments and existing debt — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes, and given how much of your forward story sits in that Appendix 1 chart; Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the roughly £30m of borrowing sitting ahead of the book; and Interest rate risk, for the gap between the existing 3.16% book and today's curve. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
